I don’t have the ability to pull live data from the web right now, so I can’t return the exact hourly forecast for those coordinates at this moment. However, you can obtain exactly what you’re looking for yourself—here’s a quick guide on how to query a public weather‑API (Open Meteo) and extract the information you asked about. --- ### 1️⃣ What You Need | Item | Why | |------|-----| | **Latitude / Longitude** | `lat=37.8651`, `lon=-119.5383` | | **Hourly variables** | Temperature (`temperature_2m`)
Wind speed (`windspeed_10m`)
Precipitation (`rainfall`) | | **Date range** | Today + next 9 days → total 10 days | | **Timezone** | Optional – set to your local zone or UTC | --- ### 2️⃣ Example URL ```text https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast? latitude=37.8651& longitude=-119.5383& hourly=temperature_2m,windspeed_10m,rainfall& start_date={START}& end_date={END}& timezone=auto ``` Replace `{START}` and `{END}` with dates in ISO format (`YYYY-MM-DD`). If today is *2026‑05‑18*, then: * `start_date=2026-05-18` * `end_date=2026-05-27` Resulting full link: ```text https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=37.8651&longitude=-119.5383&hourly=temperature_2m,windspeed_10m,rainfall&start_date=2026-05-18&end_date=2026-05-27&timezone=auto ``` --- ### 3️⃣ Quick “curl” Demo ```bash curl "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=37.8651&longitude=-119.5383&hourly=temperature_2m,windspeed_10m,rainfall&start_date=$(date '+%Y-%m-%d')&end_date=$(date --date='+9 day' '+%Y-%m-%d')&timezone=auto" ``` *(On Windows PowerShell replace `$(...)` with appropriate commands.)* --- ### 4️⃣ Parsing the Response (Python) ```python import requests from datetime import datetime, timedelta base_url = ("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?" "latitude=37.8651&longitude=-119.5383" "&hourly=temperature_2m,windspeed_10m,rainfall") today = datetime.utcnow().strftime("%Y-%m-%d") future = (datetime.utcnow() + timedelta(days=9)).strftime("%Y-%m-%d") params = { "start_date": today, "end_date": future, "timezone": "auto", } resp = requests.get(base_url, params=params) data = resp.json() for t, tmp, ws, rain in zip( data["hourly"]["time"], data["hourly"]["temperature_2m"], data["hourly"]["windspeed_10m"], data["hourly"]["rainfall"]): print(f"{t}: Temp {tmp:.1f}°C, Wind {ws:.1f} km/h, Rain {rain:.1f} mm") ``` This will output one line per hour for all ten days. --- ### 5️⃣ Things To Keep In Mind | Tip | Explanation | |-----|-------------| | **Rate limits** | Free tier allows ~1000 calls/day. If you hit limits, consider caching results locally. | | **Units** | Default units: °C, km/h, mm. Add `units=imperial` to switch to Fahrenheit/FPS/inches. | | **Timezones** | Setting `timezone=auto` gives times adjusted to the location’s local time. | | **Precipitation variable** | Some models report only rainfall; others also offer snowfall. Adjust as needed. | --- #### Bottom Line While I can’t deliver the raw data directly here, the steps above let you grab the same hourly temperature, wind speed, and precipitation forecasts for the next ten days straight from a reliable source. Just plug in the URL into a browser, `curl`, Postman, or write a short script—the data comes back in clean JSON ready for whatever downstream processing you need!
